lessons.title: Welcome to the Media Lab: devices, files and folders
lessons.summary: How the Lab works — learn, create, collaborate, lead, serve — and the habits every creator needs: finding, naming and backing up your work.
objectives: You will set up your portfolio folder
You will name and organise files so you can find them later
You will know which tools you will use and their age rules
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Create a folder called `Media Lab — your name` with sub-folders: Design, Photo, Video, Writing, Portfolio
- Rename three files with the pattern `2026-10-12_poster_v1.png`
- Check the age rules for Canva and CapCut with your instructor (both expect 13+; younger members use the programme's supervised accounts)

## Understand it

The Media Lab runs on five verbs: **learn** a skill, **create** something with it, **collaborate** in a team, **lead** when it is your turn, and **serve** your community with what you make. Every session ends with something made — a sketch, a photo, a draft — because making is how creative skills grow.

Before any of that, every creator needs a system for their files. Creative work produces a lot of them: drafts, exports, photos, sound clips. Professionals lose hours, and sometimes whole projects, to messy folders. Three habits prevent it:

1. **One home for each project.** A folder per project, with the same sub-folders every time: `Design`, `Photo`, `Video`, `Writing`, `Portfolio`.
2. **Names that sort themselves.** Start file names with the date written year-month-day — `2026-10-12_poster_v1.png` — so they list in order, then say what it is and which version. Never `final.png`, `final2.png`, `finalFINAL.png`.
3. **The 3-2-1 backup rule.** Keep three copies of anything important, on two different kinds of storage (your phone and a cloud drive, say), with one somewhere other than your home. Phones get lost, dropped and stolen; work that exists in one place is work you can lose.

Know your devices too: how much free storage you have, where your camera saves photos, and how to move a file from phone to laptop. Running out of space halfway through filming is a preventable disaster.

## Key words

- **File naming convention:** an agreed pattern for naming files so they sort and can be found
- **Version:** one saved stage of a piece of work: v1, v2, v3
- **Backup:** an extra copy kept somewhere else in case the original is lost
- **3-2-1 rule:** three copies, two kinds of storage, one kept away from home

## Read and watch

- [Back up your data](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/top-tips-for-staying-secure-online/always-back-up-your-most-important-data) — UK National Cyber Security Centre
- [File naming conventions](https://datamanagement.hms.harvard.edu/plan-design/file-naming-conventions) — Harvard Medical School Data Management

- **If you already can:** make a second version for a different audience or platform, and explain the choices you changed.

lessons.title: Staying safe online, and asking before you post
lessons.summary: Your digital footprint, privacy settings, and the rule this Lab lives by: never photograph, film or post a person — especially a child — without permission.
objectives: You will check the privacy settings on an account you use
You will explain what consent means for photos and videos
You will recognise a scam or unsafe message
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Complete one Be Internet Awesome activity
- Write three rules for your Creative Team about posting people's photos
- **With an AI assistant —** AI can draft a post schedule; you decide what is true, kind and safe to share. Never share someone's image or details without consent, with or without AI.

## Understand it

Your **digital footprint** is everything about you that exists online — what you post, what others post about you, what you like and comment on, and what apps collect quietly. It is very hard to delete. A screenshot can keep a post alive years after you removed it, so a good test before posting is: *would I be comfortable with my family, my teacher and a future employer seeing this?*

Protect yourself with a few settings:

- Set accounts to **private** where you can, and review who follows you.
- Turn off **location** sharing in posts and in your camera, so photos do not reveal where you live or go to school.
- Use a **strong, different password** for each account — three random words joined together is easy to remember and hard to guess — and switch on two-step verification.
- Never share your password, even with a friend.

The rule the Lab lives by: **never photograph, film or post a person without their permission — and for a child, their parent's or guardian's too.** A photo can reveal a child's face, school badge and location to strangers. Organisations like NGG keep signed consent forms; if somebody has not given consent, they are not in the picture, or they are blurred.

If anything online makes you uncomfortable — a message, a request for photos, somebody pressuring you — stop, do not reply, keep a screenshot, and tell a trusted adult. You will never be in trouble for reporting it.

## Key words

- **Digital footprint:** the trail of information about you that exists online
- **Privacy settings:** the controls that decide who can see what you share
- **Consent:** clear permission given before something is done
- **Two-step verification:** a second check, like a code, on top of your password

lessons.title: Researching online and checking your sources
lessons.summary: Find information quickly and decide whether to trust it — the skill behind every article, caption and campaign you will make.
objectives: You will search with precise keywords
You will check who made a page and when
You will credit sources and images
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Research a local environmental problem and find three trustworthy sources
- For each source, write who made it and why you trust it

## Understand it

Anybody can publish anything online, so a creator's first job is to check before they share. A simple method from fact-checkers is **SIFT**:

- **Stop.** Before you share or use something, pause. Strong emotion — anger, shock, excitement — is a signal to slow down.
- **Investigate the source.** Who made this? Search the name of the website or account. Is it a news organisation, a government body, a company selling something, or a parody account?
- **Find better coverage.** Search the claim itself. Do several reliable sources report it? If only one unknown site does, be careful.
- **Trace to the original.** Quotes, photos and statistics get passed along and changed. Find where they first appeared. A reverse image search shows where a photo has been before — often a "new" photo is years old and from somewhere else.

Search smarter, too: put exact phrases in quotes (`"Egbeda youth"`), add `site:gov.ng` to search only Nigerian government sites, and use the *Tools* menu to limit results by date.

When you use facts in your own work — a poster about plastic waste, an article about your centre — note where each came from. If somebody asks "how do you know?", you should be able to show them.

## Key words

- **Source:** where a piece of information comes from
- **Misinformation:** false information shared by mistake
- **Disinformation:** false information shared on purpose to mislead
- **Reverse image search:** searching with a picture to find where else it appears

lessons.title: AI tools: what they are and how to use them honestly
lessons.summary: What AI image and writing tools can and cannot do, how to use them as a helper rather than a replacement, and when you must say you used one.
objectives: You will use an AI tool to brainstorm ideas
You will check AI output for mistakes
You will disclose AI use in your work
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Start the first chapter of Elements of AI
- Ask an AI tool for five campaign slogans about clean streets, then improve the best one yourself and note what you changed

## Understand it

AI tools that make images, write text or edit video work by learning patterns from huge amounts of existing material, then producing something new that *fits* those patterns. That explains both what they are good at and where they fail:

- **Good at:** quick variations, brainstorming many ideas, rough drafts, tidying grammar, suggesting colour palettes or headlines.
- **Bad at:** facts (they produce confident sentences that are simply wrong), local knowledge (Egbeda, your centre, your community), hands and text inside images, and anything that needs real judgement or care for people.

Use AI as a **helper, not a replacement**. A good pattern: you decide the idea, AI helps you explore options, *you* choose, check and finish. Never ask it to do the whole assignment — you would skip the very learning the Lab is for.

Three rules of honest use:

1. **Check every fact** it gives you against a reliable source.
2. **Say when you used it.** If AI generated or substantially changed part of your work, write so in the caption or credits — the same way you credit a photographer.
3. **Respect people.** Never make fake images or voices of real people, and never upload other people's photos or private information into an AI tool.

## Key words

- **Generative AI:** software that creates new text, images or sound from patterns it learnt
- **Prompt:** the instruction you give an AI tool
- **Hallucination:** a confident but false answer from an AI tool
- **Disclosure:** saying openly that you used a tool, such as AI

lessons.title: The creative process: from a brief to a finished piece
lessons.summary: Every project in the Lab follows the same loop: brief, ideas, draft, feedback, improve, deliver. Learn it on something small.
objectives: You will read a brief and list what it asks for
You will sketch at least three ideas before choosing one
You will give feedback that helps
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Read the sample brief for a school notice
- Sketch three thumbnail ideas on paper
- **With an AI assistant —** ask it to improve one paragraph, then compare it with yours and keep what sounds like you. Check every fact — AI can state wrong things confidently.

## Understand it

Every piece of creative work — a poster, a video, a campaign — goes round the same loop. Learning the loop on something small makes big projects manageable:

1. **Brief.** What is it, who is it for, what should they do or feel, and by when? A good brief fits in three sentences. If you cannot write it, you do not yet know what you are making.
2. **Ideas.** Make many, quickly, before choosing. Sketch ten rough thumbnails in ten minutes; the first idea is rarely the best one.
3. **Draft.** Build the strongest idea roughly. Do not polish yet.
4. **Feedback.** Show the draft to somebody — ideally somebody like the audience — and ask specific questions: *What do you notice first? What is this asking you to do?*
5. **Improve.** Change what the feedback revealed. Keep what works.
6. **Deliver.** Finish properly: right size, right format, spell-checked, named correctly, on time.

The loop can go round more than once. Professionals expect it to: a designer might show a client three rounds of drafts.

Taking feedback is a skill. Listen without arguing, say thank you, and then decide — not every suggestion must be used, but every one is information about how your work is seen.

## Key words

- **Creative brief:** a short statement of what is being made, for whom and why
- **Thumbnail sketch:** a tiny, quick drawing to test an idea
- **Iteration:** improving work by going round the loop again
- **Deliverable:** the finished thing you hand over

lessons.title: Creative Teams: roles and how we work together
lessons.summary: Teams of designer, editor, photographer, writer, social media lead and project lead — with roles that rotate, so everybody finds their strengths.
objectives: You will join a Creative Team and take a first role
You will agree team rules
You will plan who does what on a small task
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Meet your team and agree three team rules
- Choose your first role — it rotates each month

## Understand it

Real media work is done in teams, and the Lab's Creative Teams copy how a small studio is organised:

- **Project lead** — keeps the plan, the deadlines and the team talking.
- **Designer** — graphics, layout and the look of everything.
- **Photographer** — still images, and the permissions that go with them.
- **Editor** — video editing and checking quality before anything goes out.
- **Writer** — headlines, captions, articles and scripts.
- **Social media lead** — where and when work is published, and how people respond.

Roles **rotate**, so everybody tries every job. You may discover you love something you would never have chosen.

Teams that work well do a few simple things. They agree the plan at the start and write it down. Everybody knows exactly what they owe and by when. They check in briefly every session — *what did I do, what am I doing next, what is blocking me?* — and they raise problems early, not on the deadline. Disagreements are about the work, never the person: "I think the title is hard to read in yellow" not "your design is bad".

Every member's work is credited. A finished project lists who did what.

## Key words

- **Role:** a person's job within a team
- **Stand-up / check-in:** a short meeting where each person says what they did, will do, and what blocks them
- **Credit:** naming who made each part of a piece of work

lessons.title: Graphic design 1: Canva and visual hierarchy
lessons.summary: Make one thing on the page the most important — through size, colour and position — so people see the message first.
objectives: You will set up a design in Canva
You will use size and contrast to show what matters most
You will export a design correctly
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Do the Canva Design School beginner lesson
- Recreate a poster you like to understand its structure
- **With an AI assistant —** try Canva Magic tools for a first idea, then make it your own: original, readable and on-brand. Do not use AI images of real people, or logos you do not own.

## Understand it

**Visual hierarchy** is the order in which a viewer notices things. A designer decides that order on purpose, so the most important message is seen first — usually in under three seconds as somebody walks past a poster or scrolls past a post.

You create hierarchy with:

- **Size** — the biggest thing is seen first.
- **Colour and contrast** — a bright or dark element stands out against a calm background.
- **Position** — people tend to look at the top first, and in left-to-right languages, scan from the top left.
- **Space** — something surrounded by empty space looks important.
- **Weight** — bold type before regular type.

A good poster usually has three levels: (1) the **headline** — the one thing to remember; (2) the **supporting** information — what, when, where; (3) the **details** — small print, logos, contact. If everything is big, nothing is.

**Canva** is a free design tool that runs in a browser or app. Start from a blank design at the right size rather than a busy template, so the decisions are yours. Use its alignment guides, and the *Position* tool to line items up exactly. A quick check for hierarchy: step back and squint at your screen. The shapes that still stand out are what people will see first.

## Key words

- **Visual hierarchy:** the order in which a viewer notices parts of a design
- **Headline:** the main, most important line of text
- **Contrast:** difference between elements in size, colour or weight
- **Squint test:** blurring your view to see which parts stand out

lessons.summary: Your team makes three posters about one local environmental problem, using what you researched in week 2.
objectives: You will deliver a set of three consistent posters
You will credit your sources

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Plan the three posters as a team
- Design them in Canva
- Present them at the next session

## Understand it

An awareness campaign tries to change what people **know**, **feel** or **do** about a problem. A poster set — three posters that clearly belong together — repeats one message in different ways so it sticks.

Plan before designing:

1. **One problem, one place.** "Plastic bags blocking the gutters on our street" is stronger than "pollution". Use what you found in your research in week 2, with sources.
2. **One action.** What should people do after seeing it? "Bring your own bag to the market" is an action; "save the planet" is not.
3. **Three angles.** Poster 1 states the problem with a striking fact; poster 2 shows the effect on people; poster 3 gives the action.

Make them a **set**: the same colours, the same fonts, the same layout grid and logo position on all three. Change the image and the headline; keep everything else consistent.

Check facts, credit any photos you did not take, and only use images you are allowed to use — your own, or free-licence sources such as Unsplash or Pexels. Finally, the 3-second test: show each poster to someone for three seconds and ask what it was about. If they cannot say, the headline needs to be bigger or simpler.

## Key words

- **Awareness campaign:** communication that aims to change what people know, feel or do
- **Call to action:** the specific thing you ask the audience to do
- **Series / set:** several pieces designed to clearly belong together

lessons.title: Colour
lessons.summary: How colour sets mood and meaning, how to build a palette, and how to keep text readable.
objectives: You will build a three-colour palette
You will explain what different colours suggest
You will check text contrast
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Do the Canva colour lesson
- Build a palette for an imaginary juice brand

## Understand it

Colour works on feelings before people read a word. Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel energetic and urgent; cool colours (blue, green, purple) feel calm and trustworthy. Meanings also depend on culture and context — white is weddings in some places and mourning in others; green is Nigeria's flag and also "go" and "nature". Ask what your colours will mean to *your* audience.

The **colour wheel** helps build palettes that work:

- **Complementary** — opposite colours (blue and orange): strong contrast, good for a highlight.
- **Analogous** — neighbours (blue, teal, green): calm and harmonious.
- **Monochrome** — shades of one colour: elegant and simple.

A practical palette for most designs is the **60-30-10** rule: 60% a main, quiet colour (often the background), 30% a secondary colour, and 10% a bright accent saved for the most important thing — the headline or the button.

Above all, text must be **readable**. Dark text on a light background, or light on dark, with strong contrast. Yellow text on white, or red on green, fails — and about 1 in 12 men cannot easily tell red from green at all. Check contrast with a contrast checker: aim for at least 4.5:1 for normal text.

## Key words

- **Colour wheel:** a circle of colours showing how they relate
- **Complementary colours:** colours opposite each other on the wheel
- **Palette:** the small set of colours a design uses
- **60-30-10 rule:** a balance of main, secondary and accent colour

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Redesign a crowded flyer using only two fonts

## Understand it

Typography — the choice and arrangement of type — carries most of a design's message, because most designs are mostly words.

Typefaces come in families with different personalities:

- **Serif** fonts have small "feet" on the letters (like Times New Roman): traditional, serious, bookish.
- **Sans-serif** fonts have none (like Arial, Montserrat): clean, modern, easy to read on screens.
- **Display** and **script** fonts are decorative: use them only for a few large words, never for paragraphs.

Pairing rules that rarely fail: use **at most two** typefaces; pair contrasting ones (a bold sans headline with a clean serif body, or one sans family in different weights); and keep body text in a plain, readable font.

Size and spacing matter as much as the font:

- Make the headline clearly bigger — at least twice the body size — so the hierarchy is obvious.
- Leave enough space between lines (**leading**) — about 1.3 to 1.5 times the text size for body text.
- Avoid ALL CAPITALS for more than a few words; they are harder to read.
- Align text to the left for paragraphs; centred text is fine for a short headline.

Test your design at its real size — on a phone screen, or printed — not zoomed in on your editor.

## Key words

- **Typeface / font:** a design of letters / one size and style of it
- **Serif / sans-serif:** letters with small feet / without them
- **Leading:** the space between lines of text
- **Font pairing:** choosing two typefaces that work together

lessons.summary: Alignment, margins and a simple grid make a design look intentional and calm.
objectives: You will align elements to a grid

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Use Canva's grid to rebuild a busy page

## Understand it

Designs look professional when things line up. That is the job of **layout**: deciding where everything goes so the design feels calm and intentional rather than scattered.

Four principles:

- **Alignment.** Every element should line up with something else. Choose a few strong edges — the left margin, the centre — and stick to them.
- **Margins.** Leave an empty border around the whole design. Text crammed to the edge looks cheap and may be cut off when printed.
- **Proximity.** Put related things close together and unrelated things apart. The date, time and place belong in one group; the logo sits on its own.
- **White space.** Empty space is not wasted; it lets the important things breathe.

A **grid** makes all of this easier. Divide the page into columns (a simple 2, 3 or 4 columns) with equal gaps, and place everything on those columns. Magazines, websites and posters are built on grids even when you cannot see them.

In Canva, turn on **rulers and guides** (File → View settings) and add a column grid. Then use the *Position → Align* tools rather than nudging by eye. A useful check: print your design or view it small. Anything slightly out of line, or floating with no relationship to anything else, becomes obvious.

## Key words

- **Grid:** invisible columns and rows used to place design elements
- **Alignment:** lining elements up along shared edges or centres
- **Proximity:** grouping related items close together
- **Margin:** the empty border around a design

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Design an Instagram post announcing a centre open day
- **With an AI assistant —** AI can draft a post schedule; you decide what is true, kind and safe to share. Never share someone's image or details without consent, with or without AI.

## Understand it

A social media graphic combines everything so far — hierarchy, colour, type and layout — in a small space that people see for about a second while scrolling.

Start with the **right size** for the platform. Common ones:

- Instagram feed post: 1080 × 1350 px (portrait, 4:5) or 1080 × 1080 (square)
- Instagram or WhatsApp Status / Stories: 1080 × 1920 (9:16)
- X (Twitter) or LinkedIn post image: about 1200 × 675 (16:9)

Then design for the **scroll**:

- **One message.** A single short headline — six words or fewer is ideal. Details go in the caption, not the image.
- **Large type**, readable on a phone at arm's length.
- **A strong focal point** — one image or shape that catches the eye.
- **Safe zones.** Stories have buttons and profile names over the top and bottom; keep text away from the edges.
- **Brand consistency** — the same fonts, colours and logo position as your other posts, so people recognise you before they read.

Compose with intention: place the most important thing on a strong point (a third of the way in, or the centre), and use lines and shapes to lead the eye to the message. Export as PNG for graphics with text, and preview it on a real phone before posting.

## Key words

- **Aspect ratio:** the shape of an image as width to height, like 4:5 or 9:16
- **Focal point:** the place the eye goes first
- **Safe zone:** the area clear of app buttons and overlays
- **Composition:** how elements are arranged within the frame

lessons.title: Branding basics: logos and identity
lessons.summary: A brand is a promise people recognise: a name, a logo, colours and a voice used consistently.
objectives: You will explain what a brand identity includes
You will sketch logo ideas

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Study two local brands and list their colours, fonts and tone
- **With an AI assistant —** try Canva Magic tools for a first idea, then make it your own: original, readable and on-brand. Do not use AI images of real people, or logos you do not own.

## Understand it

A **brand** is what people think and feel when they meet an organisation — and it is built by being recognisably the same every time. The visible parts are its **identity**:

- **Name** — short, easy to say and spell, and not already used by someone else.
- **Logo** — a simple mark that works small (on a phone screen, a badge) and in one colour. The best logos are simple shapes: if you cannot draw it from memory, it is too complicated.
- **Colours** — two to four, used consistently.
- **Typefaces** — one or two.
- **Voice** — how it speaks: friendly, formal, playful, serious.

Logos come in a few types: a **wordmark** (the name in a particular font, like Google), a **symbol** (a picture, like Apple's apple), or a **combination** of both.

The tool that keeps a brand consistent is a **brand guide**: one page that shows the logo and its versions (full colour, black, white), the exact colour codes, the fonts, and a few rules — the space to leave around the logo, what not to do (stretch it, change its colours, put it on a busy photo). Everyone who makes something for the brand follows the guide, which is why big brands look the same everywhere.

Respect other people's brands, too: copying a logo, or making one too similar to a famous one, can break trademark law.

## Key words

- **Brand:** what people think and feel about an organisation
- **Brand identity:** the visible parts: name, logo, colours, type, voice
- **Wordmark:** a logo made from the name in a particular typeface
- **Brand guide:** the rules for using a brand's identity consistently

## What to do

- Design an invitation and a certificate for a Media Lab event

## Understand it

Invitations and certificates look simple, but they test everything you know about hierarchy, type and layout, because they carry a lot of information that must be easy to find.

**An invitation** must answer: *what is it, who is it from, when, where, and what should I do?* Give these a clear order:

1. The event's name — the biggest text.
2. Date, time and place — grouped together, clear and easy to find.
3. Who is inviting — usually with a logo.
4. What to do — "RSVP to 0803 … by 20 November", a dress code, what to bring.

Match the tone to the event: a graduation feels formal, a community games day playful. The fonts, colours and wording all carry that tone.

**A certificate** honours somebody, so it should feel dignified and permanent:

- The person's **name** is the most important element — large, often in a refined font.
- What it is for, written precisely: "for completing the Media Lab Foundation Programme, 2026".
- The organisation, its logo, the date, and space for signatures.
- Generous margins and a simple border; symmetry (centred layout) suits certificates.

Always double-check spelling — especially names. A misspelt name on a certificate is the one mistake the recipient will remember.

## Key words

- **Information hierarchy:** putting information in order of importance
- **Tone:** the feeling a design gives: formal, playful, serious
- **Symmetry:** a balanced, mirror-like layout around the centre
- **RSVP:** a request to reply saying whether you will come

**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Write the brief for your event as a team
- List every item you will deliver and who owns it

## Understand it

A **brand package** is every piece an event needs, all designed as one family. Planning it well is half the work.

Start with **who and what**:

- *The event:* what it is, when and where, and what makes it special.
- *The audience:* who should come, and what would make them want to?
- *The feeling:* three words for how it should feel — "proud, joyful, local".

Then list the **deliverables** and their sizes — for example: logo (with colour and one-colour versions), colour palette, A3 poster, Instagram post (1080 × 1350), WhatsApp Status (1080 × 1920), invitation, name badge.

Make a **moodboard**: a single page of images, colours, textures and type that capture the feeling. It lets the team agree on a direction *before* anybody designs, which avoids arguments later.

Finally, divide the work: who owns each deliverable, who reviews it, and the deadline. Agree on shared files first — the logo, the colour codes, the fonts — in one shared folder, so everybody builds on the same foundations. A brand package where the poster and the badge use slightly different greens looks like two different events.

## Key words

- **Brand package:** the full set of designed pieces for one brand or event
- **Moodboard:** a collage that captures the intended look and feeling
- **Deliverables list:** every piece to be made, with its size and owner

## Understand it

Today the plan becomes a package. Work **from the core outwards**:

1. **Logo first.** Everything else depends on it. Make sure it works small (badge size), in one colour, and on light and dark backgrounds.
2. **Palette and type next.** Fix the exact colour codes and fonts and put them in your team's shared folder — or a Canva Brand Kit — so everybody uses the same ones.

What makes a package feel like one family: the same colours used in the same roles (for example, navy for backgrounds, gold for highlights), the same typefaces in the same hierarchy, the logo always in the same place, and a repeated visual element — a shape, a pattern, a photo style.

Before you present, do a **consistency check**: lay every piece side by side. Do they clearly belong together? Is every fact the same on every piece — date, time, venue, spelling? lessons.summary: The rule of thirds, leading lines, angles and filling the frame — on the phone you already have.
objectives: You will use the rule of thirds

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Turn on your phone camera's grid
- Take five photographs of one object from different angles
- **With an AI assistant —** AI can enhance a photo, but say when an image has been changed. Never use AI to alter a real person's photo without their permission.

## Understand it

The camera you already carry is good enough. What makes a strong photograph is **composition** — what you include, what you leave out, and where you put things in the frame.

- **Rule of thirds.** Turn on your camera's grid. Place the subject on one of the lines or where two lines cross, rather than dead centre. It usually feels more alive.
- **Leading lines.** Roads, fences, rows of chairs and shadows lead the eye into the picture and towards the subject.
- **Fill the frame.** Get closer. Most beginner photos have the subject too small, surrounded by distractions. If it is not helping, leave it out.
- **Angles.** Shooting from low makes a subject look powerful; from high, smaller. Crouch down to a child's eye level instead of pointing down at them.
- **Background.** Check behind the subject before you press: a pole growing out of somebody's head, a messy bin, bright light. Move yourself to change it.
- **Framing.** Use doorways, windows and branches to frame the subject.

Take many shots and vary them — wide (where are we?), medium (what is happening?), close (detail and emotion). Then choose your best. Professionals take dozens of photographs to get one great one.

## Key words

- **Composition:** arranging what is in the frame
- **Rule of thirds:** placing subjects on lines dividing the frame into thirds
- **Leading lines:** lines in a scene that guide the eye
- **Wide / medium / close shot:** showing the place / the action / the detail

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Take three photos of the same thing — in shade, in sunlight and against a window

## Understand it

Photography means "drawing with light", and light changes a photo more than any camera does.

- **Direction.** Light from the side shows shape and texture. Light from behind you, onto the subject's face, is even and clear but can be flat. Light from behind the subject creates silhouettes and glowing edges.
- **Hard and soft light.** Midday sun in Lagos is *hard*: dark shadows under eyes and noses, squinting faces, burnt-out white areas. *Soft* light — in open shade, on an overcast day, or near a window — is kind to faces and shows detail.
- **Time of day.** The hour after sunrise and before sunset (the **golden hour**) gives warm, low, soft light. Midday is the hardest time for portraits; move into shade.

Practical habits:

- For people outdoors at midday, stand them in **open shade** — under a tree or a building's overhang — facing out towards the bright area.
- **Tap to focus and expose** on your phone screen on the subject's face, then slide the brightness slider down a little if the sky is too bright.
- Avoid the phone's flash for people close-up; it flattens faces. Find better light instead.
- Indoors, put your subject near a window and turn off mixed coloured bulbs.

When you look at any photo, ask: *where is the light coming from?* Answering that is how photographers learn.

## Key words

- **Hard / soft light:** light that makes sharp, dark shadows / gentle, gradual ones
- **Golden hour:** the warm, low light just after sunrise and before sunset
- **Exposure:** how bright or dark a photo is
- **Open shade:** shade with an open view to bright sky, giving soft light

objectives: You will ask permission before photographing anyone
You will frame a flattering portrait
You will know when a photo must not be shared
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Practise portraits of a teammate who agrees
- Review the Lab's consent rules from week 1

## Understand it

A portrait shows a person — ideally something true about them. Good portraits come from **respect** as much as technique.

**Ask first, always.** Explain who you are, what the photo is for and where it will appear. Accept "no" happily. For anybody under 18, you also need their parent's or guardian's permission, and at NGG that means a signed consent form. If you cannot get consent, do not photograph them, or photograph them so they cannot be identified.

**Put people at ease.** Chat before you lift the camera. Tell them what you are doing. Show them a shot on your screen. Relaxed people make better portraits than posed, nervous ones. Give simple directions: "turn your shoulders slightly towards the window", "look at me and think of your favourite food".

**Technique:**

- Use soft light — open shade or a window.
- Focus on the **eyes**; in portrait mode, tap on the nearest eye.
- Shoot at eye level, and slightly further away with a little zoom (2×) rather than close with wide angle, which distorts faces.
- Keep the background simple and uncluttered.

Afterwards, let the person see the photos and remove any they dislike. A portrait should leave its subject feeling respected — that is the test of whether you did it well.

## Key words

- **Portrait:** a photograph of a person that shows something about them
- **Model release / consent form:** written permission to use someone's image
- **Portrait mode:** a phone setting that blurs the background behind a person

- [Learn and explore photography](https://www.nikonusa.com/learn-and-explore) — Nikon

lessons.title: Editing photos
lessons.summary: Crop, straighten, adjust light and colour — and know when editing becomes misleading.
objectives: You will crop and straighten a photo
You will adjust exposure and colour
You will avoid misleading edits
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Edit three of your photos in a free phone editor or Canva

## Understand it

Editing turns a good photo into a finished one. Work in this order, because each step affects the next:

1. **Crop and straighten.** Remove distractions at the edges and fix a tilted horizon. Crop to the size you need (4:5 for an Instagram post).
2. **Exposure.** Make the photo as bright as it should be — not brighter.
3. **Contrast, highlights and shadows.** Bring back detail in a bright sky (lower the highlights) or a dark face (raise the shadows).
4. **Colour.** Fix colour casts — the orange of indoor bulbs, the blue of shade — with **white balance** or temperature. Adjust saturation gently; overdone colour looks fake.
5. **Sharpen** a little last.

Free tools that do all of this well: Snapseed and Google Photos on phones, Lightroom's free mobile version, Canva's photo editor.

**Edit honestly.** Improving light and colour is editing. Adding or removing people or objects, changing what happened, or making someone look different from reality turns a photograph into a misleading one. News photographers and journalists follow strict rules: no adding or removing content. For documentary and community work in the Lab, follow those rules too. If you make a creative composite, say so.

Always keep the original file. Edits should be done on a copy so you can start again.

## Key words

- **Crop:** cutting away the edges of an image
- **White balance:** correcting colours so whites look white
- **Saturation:** how strong colours are
- **Non-destructive editing:** editing that keeps the original unchanged

lessons.title: Writing for media: captions, articles and slogans
lessons.summary: Short, clear writing that people actually read — captions, a short article, a campaign slogan.
objectives: You will write a caption that adds to a photo
You will write a 150-word article
You will write and test slogans
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Write captions for three of your photos
- Write a 150-word article about something at your centre

## Understand it

Media writing is short because people read it quickly, on a phone, between other things. Every word must earn its place.

**Captions** tell people what a picture cannot: who, what, where, when — and why it matters. "Kemi, 13, tests the water filter her team built at Egbeda centre on Saturday" is a caption. "Fun day!!" is not. Name people only with their permission, and never give a child's school or home area.

**A short article** puts the most important facts first. Journalists call it the **inverted pyramid**: the first sentence answers who, what, when, where and why; the next paragraphs add detail; the least important comes last. If a reader stops after one paragraph, they still have the story. Use quotes from real people, checked with them, and short paragraphs of one to three sentences.

**Slogans** are a few memorable words: rhythm, repetition, a promise or a challenge. "Bring a bag, save a gutter." Say them out loud; good ones are easy to say.

For all three: use plain words ("use", not "utilise"), active verbs ("the team built", not "was built by the team"), and cut every word that does not add meaning. Then read it aloud — your ear catches what your eye misses.

## Key words

- **Caption:** the text that explains a photo
- **Inverted pyramid:** news writing with the most important facts first
- **Slogan:** a short, memorable phrase for a campaign or brand
- **Active voice:** the doer comes first: "the team built the filter"

lessons.title: Storytelling
lessons.summary: Beginning, middle and end; a person, a problem and a change — the shape behind every good story, photo essay or video.
objectives: You will plan a story in three parts
You will choose five images that tell it
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Plan a five-photo story about a person in your community (with their permission)

## Understand it

Nearly every story that holds attention has the same shape: **a person, a problem and a change**. Somebody wants something, something stands in the way, and by the end something is different — the situation, or the person.

The classic three acts:

1. **Beginning.** Introduce the person and their world. Make us care: a name, a face, a detail.
2. **Middle.** The problem or challenge, and what they try. Tension keeps us watching or reading.
3. **End.** What changed, and what it means. Leave the audience with a feeling or a thought.

Good storytellers also **show rather than tell**. "She was determined" tells. "She walked to the borehole twice before school, every day, for a year" shows — and the audience reaches the conclusion themselves, which makes it stronger.

True stories carry responsibility. Get the facts right, quote people accurately, let them tell their story in their own words where possible, and avoid presenting people only as victims who need saving — show their own strength and choices. Ask: *would the people in this story recognise themselves and feel respected?*

The same shape works for a photo essay, a short video, a campaign or a speech.

## Key words

- **Three-act structure:** beginning, middle and end — set-up, conflict, resolution
- **Protagonist:** the person the story follows
- **Show, don't tell:** letting details and actions reveal meaning
- **Narrative:** a connected series of events told as a story

lessons.title: Planning the photo story
lessons.summary: Plan the Month 3 challenge as a team: the story, the shots, the people to ask, and the words.
objectives: You will plan a shoot
You will get consent before the shoot
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Agree your story and shot list
- Get permission from everyone who will appear
- **With an AI assistant —** AI can enhance a photo, but say when an image has been changed. Never use AI to alter a real person's photo without their permission.

## Understand it

A **photo story** (or photo essay) tells one true story in a small sequence of images with captions. Planning makes the difference between a set of nice photos and a story.

1. **Find the story.** Look for a person or small group in your community doing something with a beginning, middle and end: a tailor finishing an order, a team preparing for a match, a grandmother teaching a recipe. Small and specific beats big and vague.
2. **Get permission early** — from every person who will appear, and from parents or guardians for children. Explain where it will be shown.
3. **Write a shot list.** A good photo story mixes:
   - an **establishing** shot — the place;
   - a **portrait** — the main person;
   - **action** shots — what they do;
   - **details** — hands, tools, faces;
   - **interaction** — people together;
   - a **closing** shot — the result or the feeling.
4. **Plan the words.** Who will interview the person for captions? Write down facts and quotes accurately.
5. **Divide the roles** — photographer(s), writer, permission lead, editor — and set times.

Visit at the right time of day for light, and plan to shoot far more than you need.

## Key words

- **Photo essay:** a sequence of photographs that tells a story
- **Shot list:** a planned list of the photos you need
- **Establishing shot:** an image that shows where the story happens

lessons.summary: Five to eight photographs with captions that tell one true story from your community.
objectives: You will deliver a captioned photo story
You will present it to the group
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Shoot, edit and caption your story
- Present it at the next session

## Understand it

Editing a photo story is as important as shooting it. You will have far more photos than you need; choosing is where the story is made.

**Select.** Lay out all your images. First remove anything blurred, badly lit or showing a person without consent. Then pick the strongest five to eight that, in order, tell the story from beginning to end. Every photo must add something new; if two show the same thing, keep the better one.

**Sequence.** Start with a strong opening image that makes people want to look further. Vary wide, medium and close shots so the rhythm does not get monotonous. End on an image with feeling or a sense of conclusion.

**Edit consistently** — similar colour and brightness across all photos, so they look like one set.

**Write the captions.** The first caption introduces the person and the story; the others add what each picture cannot show. Check every name, fact and quote with the people involved.

**Present it** — as a printed display, a slideshow, or a carousel post — with a title and the credits: who photographed, who wrote, who edited. Then show it to the people in it before sharing it more widely. It is their story; they should see it first.

## Key words

- **Sequencing:** choosing the order of images to tell a story
- **Edit (selection):** choosing which images to keep
- **Carousel:** a social media post of several swipeable images

lessons.title: Video 1: storyboarding
lessons.summary: Plan every shot before you film — it saves hours of editing.
objectives: You will storyboard a one-minute video
You will plan shot types (wide, medium, close-up)
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Storyboard a one-minute 'day at the centre' video in six frames
- **With an AI assistant —** Use AI to suggest a shot list or captions, then check every caption against what is actually said. Label AI-generated footage or voices honestly.

## Understand it

A **storyboard** is a comic-strip plan of a video: one small drawing for each shot, in order, with notes. Every film studio uses them, because thinking on paper is free and thinking while filming wastes everyone's time — and editing footage you never planned is slow and frustrating.

Each frame of a storyboard records:

- **The shot size** — wide (shows the whole place), medium (a person from the waist up), close-up (a face), extreme close-up (hands, eyes, a detail).
- **The angle** — eye level, low, high.
- **Movement** — is the camera still, or does it pan (turn) or follow?
- **What happens** and **what is heard** — the action, the words, the sounds or music.
- **Roughly how long** it lasts.

Stick figures are fine; a storyboard is a plan, not art. What matters is that someone else could read it and film your video.

Good sequences change shot size: wide to set the scene, then medium to show the action, then close-up for emotion. Two shots of the same size from the same angle placed together look like a jump — vary them. Plan also for **B-roll**: extra shots of the place and details, which you will lay over interviews and use to cover cuts. Editors always wish they had more of it.

## Key words

- **Storyboard:** a sequence of drawings planning each shot of a video
- **Shot size:** how much of the subject fills the frame: wide, medium, close-up
- **Pan:** turning the camera left or right from one spot
- **B-roll:** extra footage used over interviews or to cover cuts

lessons.title: Video 2: shooting on a phone
lessons.summary: Steady shots, landscape or portrait on purpose, good light and clean sound.
objectives: You will film steady shots
You will capture clear sound
You will film the shots on your storyboard
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Film the six shots from your storyboard

## Understand it

A modern phone films excellent video if you handle it well. The difference between amateur and professional-looking phone video is mostly habits:

**Steady.** Hold the phone with both hands, elbows tucked in to your body, or rest it on something solid — a wall, a table, a bag. Move your whole body slowly rather than waving the phone. A cheap tripod or phone clamp transforms results.

**Orientation on purpose.** Film **vertical** (9:16) for Stories, Reels, TikTok and WhatsApp Status; **horizontal** (16:9) for YouTube, presentations and screens. Decide before you press record — you cannot turn a vertical clip into a good horizontal one.

**Light.** Face your subject towards the light; never film someone standing in front of a bright window. Avoid harsh midday sun on faces.

**Sound — the part beginners forget.** Audiences forgive average pictures but not bad sound. Get the phone close to the person speaking (within an arm's length), film somewhere quiet, away from generators, traffic and fans. A small clip-on microphone is the best money a creator spends.

**Settings.** Lock focus and exposure (tap and hold on the subject), clean the lens with a soft cloth, and record a few extra seconds before and after each action — editors need those handles to cut smoothly.

## Key words

- **Stabilisation:** keeping the camera steady while filming
- **Aspect ratio:** the shape of the frame: 9:16 vertical, 16:9 horizontal
- **Lavalier (lav) mic:** a small clip-on microphone
- **Handles:** extra seconds recorded before and after the action

lessons.summary: Cut, trim, order and pace your clips in CapCut or DaVinci Resolve.
objectives: You will import and trim clips

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Edit your clips into a one-minute video
- **With an AI assistant —** Use AI to suggest a shot list or captions, then check every caption against what is actually said. Label AI-generated footage or voices honestly.

## Understand it

Editing is where a video's story is really written. The basic actions:

- **Import** your clips and organise them — delete obvious failures first.
- **Trim** each clip so it starts and ends at the right moment. Cut the fumbling start and the drifting end.
- **Arrange** clips on the **timeline** in story order.
- **Cut** to change shots. Most cuts in professional video are plain, simple cuts — fancy transitions draw attention to themselves and usually look amateur.

**Pacing** is how fast the video feels. Social video moves quickly: most shots last two to five seconds, and the first two seconds must hook the viewer. Documentary and emotional moments can breathe longer. Cut when a shot has shown what it needs to — not when it runs out.

Useful techniques:

- **Cut on action** — cut from one shot to the next in the middle of a movement (a door opening, a hand reaching); it hides the cut.
- **J- and L-cuts** — let the sound of the next shot start before its picture, or the sound of the last shot carry on under the new picture. It makes edits flow.

Free editors: **CapCut** (phone and computer) and **DaVinci Resolve** (computer, professional). Save your project often, and keep all the clips for one project in one folder before you start, so nothing goes "missing" from the timeline.

## Key words

- **Timeline:** where clips are arranged in order in an editor
- **Trim:** shortening a clip's start or end
- **Pacing:** how fast or slow a video feels
- **Cut on action:** cutting during a movement so the edit is unnoticed

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Add music and subtitles to your one-minute video

## Understand it

Sound is half of video. Three layers make up a soundtrack:

1. **Dialogue** — people speaking. It must be clear. Adjust levels so voices are steady, and remove hum or wind noise where your editor allows.
2. **Music** — sets mood and pace. Keep it well **under** speech; dip it lower whenever someone talks.
3. **Sound effects and atmosphere** — the background of the place, which makes it feel real.

**Music you are allowed to use.** Songs from the radio or the charts are protected by **copyright**: using them without a licence can get your video muted, blocked or removed, and it is not fair to the artists. Use music that is free to use — the **YouTube Audio Library**, the music libraries inside CapCut and editing apps, or Creative Commons tracks whose licence allows your use — and credit the artist as the licence asks.

**Subtitles** (captions) are essential:

- Deaf and hard-of-hearing people need them.
- Most people watch social video with the sound **off**.
- They help viewers follow different accents and languages.

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Write five open questions
- Record a two-minute interview with a teammate

## Understand it

An interview lets real people tell a story in their own words — the heart of most documentaries.

**Before.** Research the person and the topic. Write **open questions** that cannot be answered with yes or no: "How did the market change after the road was built?" rather than "Did the market change?". Prepare more questions than you need, and get permission — in writing for anybody under 18, with a parent or guardian's consent.

**Setting up.**

- Choose a quiet place with soft light on the speaker's face and an interesting but uncluttered background.
- Frame a **medium close-up** (head and shoulders), with the person slightly off-centre, looking **towards the interviewer**, who sits just beside the camera — not into the lens.
- Put the microphone close. Record a test and listen back with headphones.

**During.** Put the person at ease with easy questions first. Ask one question at a time, then **stay quiet** — the best answers often come after a pause. Do not say "yes" or "mm-hm" while they speak; it ends up on the recording. Ask them to answer in full sentences ("The market changed when…"), because your question will be cut out. Finish with: "Is there anything I did not ask that you would like to say?"

**After.** Thank them, tell them where it will appear, and represent what they said fairly in the edit.

## Key words

- **Open question:** a question that needs a full answer, not yes or no
- **Medium close-up:** a shot of a person's head and shoulders
- **Eyeline:** where the person on screen is looking
- **Informed consent:** permission given by someone who understands how their image and words will be used

**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Choose your topic and storyboard

## Understand it

A **documentary** tells a true story with real people and places. Two to three minutes is short, so focus is everything: **one story, one person or small group, one change**.

Plan as a team:

1. **The question.** Every good documentary answers a question the viewer cares about. "How does a young tailor in our street build her business?" is better than "a film about our community".
2. **Research** — talk to people before filming. Find your main **character** and check they are willing and able to take part, with consent.
3. **Structure** — sketch beginning, middle and end on paper. What will the opening shot be? What is the turning point? How does it end?
4. **Shot list** — interviews (who, where), and **B-roll** for each part of the story: the place, the work, hands, faces, details.
5. **Logistics** — dates, times, locations, equipment, batteries and storage, who does what. Check permission to film in each place (a market, a school, a shop).
6. **Interview questions** — written in advance.

Plan for honesty: you are showing real people to an audience. Do not stage events and present them as real, and give context so the story is fair. The best community documentaries leave the people in them feeling seen, not used.

## Key words

- **Documentary:** a non-fiction film that tells a true story
- **Character:** the real person a documentary follows
- **Logistics:** the practical planning of who, where, when and what equipment
- **Turning point:** the moment the story changes direction

lessons.summary: Shape interviews and footage into a story with a beginning, middle and end.
objectives: You will cut interviews down to the best moments

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Edit your team's documentary rough cut
- Swap rough cuts with another team for feedback
- **With an AI assistant —** Use AI to suggest a shot list or captions, then check every caption against what is actually said. Label AI-generated footage or voices honestly.

## Understand it

Editing a documentary is different from editing a planned film: the story is found in the footage.

1. **Log your footage.** Watch everything and note the best moments with their times — especially interview answers. A transcript of the interviews (auto-captions help) makes this much faster.
2. **Build a radio cut first.** Lay out only the interview answers, in order, so that the story makes sense by sound alone. This is the spine of your film. Aim for your target length, or a little longer.
3. **Cover with B-roll.** Place footage over the interviews to show what people are describing. Cutting away to B-roll also hides edits inside an answer.
4. **Shape the structure** — a strong opening that hooks (often a striking image or line, not a title card), the middle, and an ending that lands.
5. **Add music** under key moments, low under speech, and **subtitles** throughout.
6. **Watch with fresh eyes** — show it to someone who has not seen it, and notice where their attention drifts. That is where to cut.

Keep it fair: when you shorten what someone said, the meaning must stay the same. Never join two sentences in a way that changes what the person meant.

## Key words

- **Logging:** noting the content and timing of footage
- **Radio cut:** a first edit built from interview audio alone
- **Cutaway:** a shot inserted to cover a cut or show what is described
- **Rough cut / fine cut:** the first full edit / the polished final edit

## What to do

- Finish, subtitle and export

## Understand it

Finishing and delivering a documentary well is a craft of its own. Before you call it done, run through this checklist:

**Picture.** Colour and brightness are consistent from shot to shot. No accidental frames left between cuts. Titles and names spelt correctly and on screen long enough to read. Lower-thirds (the name and role of each interviewee) appear the first time each person speaks.

**Sound.** Dialogue is clear and at an even level throughout. Music never drowns out speech. No sudden loud bits. Listen once with headphones and once on a phone speaker.

**Words.** Subtitles are complete, corrected and timed.

**Credits.** Everyone who made it, everyone who appeared, music titles and artists as their licences require, and thanks to people and places that helped.

**Export** in the format the platform needs — commonly MP4 (H.264), 1080p, at the frame rate you filmed — and watch the exported file all the way through. Exports sometimes add glitches the edit did not have.

Then **screen it** to the people in it first, before anyone else. It is their story; they deserve to see it and to raise any concern. Afterwards, write a short reflection: what worked, what you would film differently, and one skill you will practise next.

## Key words

- **Lower third:** a caption in the lower part of the screen naming a speaker
- **Export / render:** creating the final video file from the edit

- **Screening:** showing a film to an audience

lessons.summary: Who is on which platform, what works where, and how to post responsibly for an organisation.
objectives: You will match content to a platform and audience
You will follow an organisation's posting rules
You will handle negative comments calmly
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Compare how three organisations post on two platforms
- **With an AI assistant —** AI can draft a post schedule; you decide what is true, kind and safe to share. Never share someone's image or details without consent, with or without AI.

## Understand it

Each social platform has its own audience, format and culture, so the same post rarely works everywhere:

- **WhatsApp** — the most used in Nigeria: Status, groups and Channels for direct, personal reach.
- **Instagram** — visual: photos, carousels, Reels and Stories.
- **TikTok** — short vertical video, trends and sound.
- **Facebook** — community groups and events, an older audience.
- **X (Twitter)** — news, conversation, short text.
- **YouTube** — longer video, tutorials, documentaries; very searchable.
- **LinkedIn** — professional: jobs, achievements, organisations.

Choose platforms by asking *where is my audience, and what do they do there?* — not by where you personally spend time.

Posting **for an organisation** is a responsibility, because everything you post speaks for it:

- Follow the organisation's rules and get approval before posting.
- **Consent** for every person shown — and never show a child's full name, school or location.
- Check facts and spelling before posting; a correction is less visible than the mistake.
- Respect copyright — only use music and images you are allowed to use.
- Reply politely to comments; never argue in public. Report and block abuse, and tell your supervisor.

Most platforms require users to be at least 13. Younger members work under supervised organisation accounts.

## Key words

- **Platform:** a social media service such as Instagram or WhatsApp
- **Audience:** the people you want to reach
- **Community guidelines:** a platform's rules about what may be posted
- **Brand voice:** how an organisation sounds when it speaks

## What to do

- Make a one-week content calendar for the Media Lab's own page

## Understand it

Posting whenever you feel like it rarely builds an audience. A **content strategy** decides *why* you post, *what*, *where* and *when*.

1. **One goal.** What should the posts achieve this week? "Get 30 families to the open day" is a goal you can measure; "raise awareness" is vague.
2. **Content pillars.** Three or four themes your posts rotate between, such as *behind the scenes*, *member stories*, *tips and skills*, *event news*. Pillars keep content varied but on-message.
3. **Formats.** Mix them: a photo, a carousel, a short video, a Story poll, a quote graphic.
4. **Timing.** Post when your audience is online — often evenings and weekends for families. Platforms' insights show when your followers are active.

A **content calendar** puts it all in a table:

| Day | Platform | Pillar | Format | Idea / caption | Owner | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

A spreadsheet is perfect. Planning a week ahead means posts are thought through, checked and approved — not rushed and full of mistakes.

Leave space for the unplanned: something happens at the centre on Saturday, and that real moment is often your best post of the week.

## Key words

- **Content strategy:** the plan for why, what, where and when you post
- **Content pillars:** the main themes your posts rotate between
- **Content calendar:** a schedule of planned posts
- **Insights / analytics:** platform data about who sees and engages with posts

lessons.summary: Audience, message, call to action, and reading simple numbers — reach, engagement, clicks.
objectives: You will write a clear call to action
You will read reach and engagement
You will explain what makes a campaign work
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Analyse one campaign you like: audience, message, call to action

## Understand it

Marketing is getting the **right message** to the **right people** so they **do something**. Every good post or campaign answers three questions:

1. **Audience** — who exactly? "Parents of 10- to 17-year-olds in Egbeda" is better than "everyone". Think about what they care about and worry about.
2. **Message** — what one thing should they understand? Speak to *their* interest, not yours: "Your child will build a real website by December" beats "We teach coding".
3. **Call to action** — what should they do next? "Send OPEN DAY to 0803 …", "Register at the link in our bio", "Share with a parent who should know". One clear action, easy to do.

Then measure, because numbers tell you what is working:

- **Reach** — how many different people saw it.
- **Impressions** — how many times it was seen in total.
- **Engagement** — likes, comments, shares, saves. **Engagement rate** = engagements ÷ reach × 100.
- **Clicks** and, best of all, **conversions** — people who actually did the action.

Compare posts against each other, not against celebrities. If one style of post gets twice the engagement of another, make more like it. And beware **vanity metrics**: a thousand likes matter less than ten families who came to the open day.

## Key words

- **Target audience:** the specific group a message is for
- **Call to action (CTA):** the one thing you ask the audience to do
- **Reach / impressions:** people who saw it / total times it was seen
- **Engagement rate:** engagements divided by reach, as a percentage

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Generate ten caption ideas with an AI tool, pick and improve two, and note what you changed

## Understand it

AI tools can speed up creative work — but the decisions, the facts and the credit must stay yours.

**Where AI genuinely helps:**

- Brainstorming — "give me 20 headline ideas for an open day aimed at parents" — then *you* choose and rewrite the best.
- Variations — resizing a design for several platforms, suggesting colour palettes, drafting alternative captions.
- Tidying — fixing grammar and spelling in your own writing.
- Planning — a first draft of a content calendar for you to adjust.

**Where it does harm:**

- **Invented facts.** AI writes confident nonsense. Check every number, date and claim.
- **Generic work.** AI output tends towards the average; your local knowledge and real photos are what make work stand out.
- **People.** Never create fake images, videos or voices of real people, and never upload other people's photos or private details to an AI tool.
- **Copying style or work.** Do not prompt for an artist's style to pass off as your own.

**Disclose it.** If AI generated or substantially changed part of a piece, say so — in the caption or credits — the same way you would credit a photographer. Many platforms now require labels on realistic AI-generated images and video.

A good test: could you explain and defend every choice in the finished piece? If not, it is not yet your work.

## Key words

- **Generative AI:** software that creates text, images or sound from patterns it learnt
- **Deepfake:** realistic fake video, image or audio of a real person
- **AI disclosure:** stating clearly that AI was used and how

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Script and storyboard a 30-second promo for an NGG centre

## Understand it

A **promotional video** makes people want to do something — come to an event, join a programme, support a cause — in 30 to 60 seconds. Its structure is simple and strict:

1. **Hook (0–3 seconds).** The most striking image, movement or line first. People decide to keep watching almost instantly. Do not start with a logo.
2. **Message (3–45 seconds).** Show, don't tell: real people doing exciting things, quick cuts, a few short on-screen words. Answer *what is it, and why should I care?* Speak to the viewer's interest.
3. **Call to action (last 5–10 seconds).** What, when, where, how — clearly on screen, long enough to read: "Open Day · Saturday 15 Nov · 10am · Egbeda Centre · Register: link in bio".

Craft details that matter:

- **Vertical (9:16)** for Reels, TikTok and Status.
- **Subtitles and text** — most people watch without sound.
- **Music** that is licensed for your use, and matches the energy.
- **Brand** — your colours, fonts and logo, consistent with the rest of the campaign.
- **Real footage** of real members, with consent.

Test it on a phone, with the sound off, with someone who knows nothing about the event. If they can tell you what it is and what to do, it works.

## Key words

- **Hook:** the opening seconds that make viewers keep watching
- **Promo:** a short video that promotes something
- **End card:** the final screen with the call to action

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Agree goal, audience and calendar
- Assign graphics, video, captions and posting
- **With an AI assistant —** AI can draft a post schedule; you decide what is true, kind and safe to share. Never share someone's image or details without consent, with or without AI.

## Understand it

A **campaign** is a set of coordinated posts over a period, all working towards one goal. Plan yours like a professional agency would:

1. **Goal** — specific and measurable: "40 registrations for the Saturday tech fair".
2. **Audience** — who, and where they are online.
3. **Key message** — one sentence the whole campaign repeats in different ways.
4. **Big idea** — the creative hook that makes the campaign memorable: a theme, a challenge, a recurring character, a hashtag.
5. **Content calendar** — a week of posts: teaser → announcement → member stories → behind the scenes → reminder → countdown → day-of.
6. **Assets list** — every graphic, the promo video, captions and sizes, each with an owner and deadline.
7. **Measurement** — what you will count (registrations, clicks, shares) and how.

Write a one-page **campaign brief** with all of this and agree it as a team before making anything. Build a shared folder with the brand assets — logo, colours, fonts — so everything matches.

Think about **sequence**: early posts build curiosity, middle posts give reasons to come, late posts create urgency. And plan for engagement — who replies to comments and messages, and how fast?

## Key words

- **Campaign:** a coordinated series of posts working towards one goal
- **Big idea:** the creative concept that ties a campaign together
- **Teaser:** an early post that builds curiosity
- **Campaign brief:** a one-page plan everyone agrees before making anything

## Understand it

Production days go smoothly when the team works like a studio:

- **Work from the brief and calendar.** Every asset has an owner, a size and a deadline. Tick them off as they are done.
- **Templates first.** Make one master graphic with the campaign's layout, fonts and colours, then duplicate it for each post. Consistency becomes automatic.
- **Batch similar work.** Shoot all the video clips in one session; design all the quote graphics together; write all the captions in one sitting. Switching between tasks wastes time.
- **Review before publishing.** Every piece is checked by someone who did not make it, against a short checklist: facts and spellings right, consent for everyone shown, brand consistent, readable on a phone, call to action clear.

**Writing captions** that work:

- The first line is the hook — it is often all people see before "…more".
- Short paragraphs, plain words, one call to action.
- A few relevant **hashtags** — your campaign tag plus two or three that your audience actually follows. Thirty random hashtags look like spam.
- **Alt text** on images where the platform allows it, for people using screen readers.

Save final files with clear names — `2026-11-10_techfair_post3_final.png` — in the shared folder, ready for whoever posts them.

- **Template:** a master design reused for consistency
- **Batching:** doing similar tasks together to save time
- **Hashtag:** a tagged keyword that groups posts on a topic

## Understand it

Today the campaign goes out and gets measured. Running a campaign is active work:

**Publish on schedule.** Follow the calendar. Many platforms let you **schedule** posts in advance, so they go out at the best time even when you are busy.

**Engage.** Social media is two-way. Reply to comments and questions quickly and politely — within a few hours is good. Like and thank people who share. Answer common questions in a pinned comment or Story.

**Watch the numbers** each day: reach, engagement, clicks on the link, and — most important — progress towards the goal (registrations). Note which posts do best and why. If one format clearly outperforms, adjust tomorrow's posts.

**Handle problems calmly.** A spelling mistake: edit or delete and repost. A negative comment: reply politely once with facts, or move the conversation to private messages; never argue. Abuse or anything unsafe: hide, report, block and tell your supervisor.

At the end, write a short **campaign report**:

- the goal and the result;
- the top three posts and why they worked;
- what did not work;
- what you would do differently next time.

Honest reports — including what failed — are what make the next campaign better.

- **Scheduling:** setting a post to publish automatically at a chosen time
- **Community management:** replying to and looking after an audience

lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Build a task board for your final project
- Run a five-minute check-in: done, doing, stuck

## Understand it

Project management is how teams finish things on time without chaos. The core is simple: **what needs doing, who is doing it, by when, and is it done?**

1. **Break the project into tasks.** "Make the documentary" is too big to act on. "Write interview questions", "book the location", "film B-roll at the market" are tasks. A good task is small enough to finish in one session and has a clear "done".
2. **Give every task one owner.** If two people own a task, nobody does.
3. **Set deadlines** — working backwards from the final date, with some spare time for the unexpected. Things always take longer than planned.
4. **Track it visibly.** A simple **Kanban board** works: three columns — *To do*, *Doing*, *Done* — with a card for each task. A whiteboard with sticky notes, a shared spreadsheet or a free tool like Trello all work.
5. **Check in regularly.** A five-minute stand-up each session: what I finished, what I am doing next, what is blocking me.

When something slips, raise it **early**. A deadline problem flagged a week ahead can be solved; flagged on the day, it cannot. Cutting scope — making something smaller but finished — is usually better than missing the deadline.

## Key words

- **Task:** a small, clear piece of work with an owner and a deadline
- **Kanban board:** a board with To do, Doing and Done columns
- **Milestone:** an important checkpoint in a project
- **Blocker:** something stopping a task from moving forward

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Teach a newer member one thing you learned (with your instructor)
- Note what you taught and how it went

## Understand it

Leadership is not being in charge; it is helping a group do its best work. In a Creative Team, the leader:

- **Makes the goal clear** — everybody can say what the team is making and why.
- **Sets the example** — on time, prepared, doing the unglamorous jobs too.
- **Shares the work fairly** and plays to people's strengths while letting them try new things.
- **Listens** — the quietest person often has the idea nobody else thought of. Ask them directly.
- **Unblocks** — notices when someone is stuck and helps, without taking over.

**Giving feedback** is a leader's most-used skill. A reliable pattern: describe the **specific** thing, its **effect**, and a **suggestion**. "The headline is pale yellow on white, so it's hard to read from a distance — try navy" helps. "It's bad" or "it's nice" does not. Praise specific things in public; raise problems in private.

**Mentoring a younger learner** is one of the best ways to master a skill yourself. Good mentors:

- Show, then let them do it — **hands off the mouse**.
- Ask questions rather than give answers: "What do you think would happen if…?"
- Break things into small steps and celebrate each one.
- Are patient with mistakes, because mistakes are how learning happens.

## Key words

- **Leadership:** helping a group achieve a shared goal
- **Constructive feedback:** specific, kind comments with a suggestion
- **Mentoring:** helping someone less experienced learn and grow
- **Delegation:** giving others responsibility for parts of the work

## Understand it

A **portfolio** is a curated collection of your best work that shows what you can do. For creative careers — and applications for scholarships, programmes and jobs — it often matters more than certificates.

**Curate, don't dump.** Choose eight to twelve of your strongest pieces, not everything. Show range — design, photography, writing, video — but only include work you are proud of. One weak piece lowers the impression of the strong ones.

**Explain each piece** in two or three sentences:

- What it is and who it was for (the brief).
- **Your role** — be honest about team projects: "I designed the poster and edited the video".
- One decision you made and why, or one problem you solved.

**Present it well.** A simple, consistent layout with your work as the star — plenty of space, no clutter. Options include a free website (Behance, Adobe Portfolio, Canva websites, GitHub Pages), a PDF, or a printed book for interviews.

**Protect privacy.** Have permission for every person shown, especially children. Remove personal details — no home address, school name or phone number; use a professional email.

Update it every few months. Replace older work as you improve — your portfolio should always show your best, current self.

## Key words

- **Portfolio:** a curated collection of your best work
- **Curation:** carefully selecting what to include
- **Case study:** a short explanation of a project: brief, role, process, result
