**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Choose your story and the formats you will use
- Agree roles — each member leads one part
- **With an AI assistant —** Use AI to suggest a shot list or captions, then check every caption against what is actually said. Label AI-generated footage or voices honestly.

## Understand it

The final challenge brings every Lab skill together: one community story told through **design, photography, writing and video** at once — like a small newsroom producing a feature.

Plan it in this order:

1. **Choose the story** — a person, group or place in your community with a real change to tell. Test it with the question: *why would someone outside our team care?*
2. **Consent** from everyone involved, in writing, with parent or guardian consent for anyone under 18.
3. **Decide the pieces**, for example:
   - a short **documentary** (2–3 minutes);
   - a **photo story** of five to eight images with captions;
   - a written **article** (about 300 words);
   - **graphics** — a poster and social posts to promote the showcase.
4. **One visual identity** — shared colours, fonts and a title treatment, so the pieces look like one project.
5. **Roles and timeline** — owners for each piece, review points, and the deadline for the showcase. Build in time for feedback and fixes.
6. **Shared folder** with clear structure and naming.

The pieces should support each other: the article can quote the interview, the photo story can show moments the video only glimpses, and the graphics invite people to see it all.

## Key words

- **Multimedia story:** one story told across several media together
- **Feature:** an in-depth story about a person, place or issue
- **Production schedule:** the timeline of who makes what, and when

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Prepare your three-minute presentation
- Rehearse with your team

## Understand it

Presenting confidently is a skill you can learn like any other.

**Structure.** A short presentation of a project follows a clear path:

1. **Hook** — open with the strongest image or a striking line from your story, not "Hello, my name is…".
2. **The story** — whose it is and why it matters, in two or three sentences.
3. **The work** — show the pieces. Let the work speak; do not read out what is on the screen.
4. **Process** — one challenge you met and how you solved it.
5. **What you learnt and what is next.**

**Slides** should be visual: big images, very few words, one idea per slide. Never paste paragraphs onto a slide.

**Delivery.**

- Rehearse out loud at least twice, with a timer, in front of someone.
- Stand steady, look at the audience, and speak a little slower and louder than feels natural.
- Pause after important points.
- Nerves are normal — even professionals feel them. Breathe out slowly before you start.

**Questions.** Listen to the whole question, repeat it if the room is big, and answer briefly. "I don't know, but I'll find out" is a fine answer.

Have a backup: your files on a USB stick and a phone, in case the projector or internet fails.

## Key words

- **Hook:** an opening that grabs attention
- **Rehearsal:** practising a presentation out loud
- **Q&A:** questions and answers after a presentation

lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Every lesson in the Lab produces something.

## What to do

- Present your project and portfolio at the showcase
- Write your next goal

## Understand it

The showcase is a celebration — of your work, your team and your community — and a chance to show families what the Lab has built this year.

**For the showcase:**

- Display or screen your final projects with titles and team credits.
- Be ready to talk to visitors about your work for a minute: what it is, what you did, what you learnt.
- Thank the people whose stories you told, and invite them if they wish to come.

**What comes next.** The Lab's pathway recognises growing skill and responsibility:

- **Junior Creator** — confidently uses the core tools and completes projects with support.
- **Creative Associate** — produces strong independent work and contributes reliably to team projects.
- **Team Lead** — plans and leads projects, mentors newer members, and takes responsibility for quality.

**Set your next goal** using what you know about yourself now. A good goal is specific and has a deadline: "Produce a three-minute documentary on my own by March" or "Lead a Creative Team for one month-long challenge".

Keep creating outside the Lab. Keep your portfolio up to date, keep your files backed up, and keep asking before you photograph or post. The habits you built this year — planning, checking, crediting and caring about the people in your stories — are what make a creator people trust.

## Key words

- **Showcase:** a public display of finished work
- **Pathway:** the stages of growing skill and responsibility in a programme
- **SMART goal:** a goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound

## Read and watch

- [SMART goals](https://www.mindtools.com/a4wo118/smart-goals) — Mind Tools
- [Google Digital Garage](https://learndigital.withgoogle.com/digitalgarage) — Google

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do the first step with your instructor or a partner, then repeat it on your own before moving on.
- **If you already can:** make a second version for a different audience or platform, and explain the choices you changed.
